newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks, bonds fall on data, dollar jumps.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks, bonds fall on data, dollar jumps.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell on Monday as investment managers adjusted portfolios on the final day of the second quarter, and the bond market slid on strong economic data.
The dollar surged to its highest level against the German mark in over three years, buoyed by concerns about European monetary union and robust U.S. economic data.

The Dow Jones industrial average lost 14.93 points to close at 7,672.79. But in the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,523 to 1,281 on heavy volume of 561 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index ended 3.92 points higher at 1,442.07.

Stocks steered a see-saw course, stumbling early Monday after surprisingly strong data on new home sales and regional manufacturing activity. The figures sent the bond market reeling and dragged stocks to sharp early losses.

"The data obviously made people wonder if the economy is picking up steam again, and that got the whole question of interest rates surfacing again," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

While few on Wall Street see another market crash on the horizon, many caution that some backtracking is inevitable, especially if the bond market worries over the strength of the economy and inflationary pressures rise.

"A 10 percent pullback at this point would be my guess," said Jack Shaughnessy, director of research at Advest. "We've had this lovely lull in the economy, and that's producing some strength in the market that's probably unsustainable."
The 30-year Treasury bond fell 17/32, or $5.31 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.79 percent from 6.74 percent on Friday. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.

The dollar rose to a peak of 1.7465 marks, its highest level since February 1994. It ended the day at 1.7455 marks, up from 1.7395 marks late Friday, buoyed by concerns about European monetary union and robust U.S. economic data.
The dollar rose to 114.68 Japanese yen from 114.61 yen.
The dollar also benefited from a series of strong U.S. economic reports Monday that suggested that growth could be picking up again after several months of slowing.

New home sales showed robust growth in May, while both Chicago and New York manufacturing indexes posted strong gains for the month of June, suggesting Tuesday's national manufacturing report from the National Association of Purchasing Management will also show strength.
On commodities exchanges, soybean prices fell sharply after the Agriculture Department said in a report that farmers had planted the largest amount of acres of soybeans in 15 years.

In other markets, corn for December delivery closed 2-3/4 cents a bushel higher at $2.38-1/4 a bushel after the government report pegged corn plantings at only 80.2 million acres, below an average of analysts' estimates for 81.8 million.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for August delivery ended up 34 cents a barrel at $19.80, with August gasoline up 0.53 cent a gallon at 58.12 cents and August heating oil up 0.38 cent a gallon at 53.85 cents. Iraqi officials confirmed its sales under a renewed deal with the United Nations would not resume until August.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,604.6, down 35.7 points, or 0.77 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,604.96, up 81.21 points, or 0.40 percent.
